report.source_text: The patient is a 40-year-old male with a history of diabetes mellitus and ethanol use who was struck by a motor vehicle while ambulating in the street. The patient presented several days after the accident with complaints of worsening back pain and difficulties on ambulation. A physical exam at the time of presentation to the Emergency Department (ED) revealed exquisite midline and sacral spinal tenderness with no significant paraspinal tenderness. The patient had subacute bruising throughout his lower extremities, torso, back, and face, with bilateral bruising over his infraorbital region (Figure 1). The patient had no saddle anesthesia or lower extremity numbness or tingling. The patient did exhibit weakness in both extremities secondary to pain; however, the range of motion was intact. CT spine showed a nondisplaced L2 vertebral body fracture (Figure 2). No acute surgical intervention was indicated as per the neurosurgical team, and the patient could be managed outpatient with a Thoracic-Lumbar-Sacral Orthosis (TLSO) brace and pain control with NSAIDs, Robaxin, and Gabapentin. Neurosurgery also recommended that the patient obtain MRI L-spine without contrast.

report.source_text: Six days after the initial presentation, the patient presented to the ED again with increasing back and left lower extremity pain, confusion, auditory hallucinations, and fever for three days. He was tachycardic to 109 bpm and febrile to 101-102F (38.8C). Neuromuscular examination demonstrated 2/5 strength in bilateral lower extremities. He was unable to perform hip flexion and leg elevation. Sensation was grossly intact throughout both lower extremities. He had a white blood cell count of 24,000/mcL with a lactate of 2.8 mmol/L.

report.source_text: Another CT scan revealed a new fluid collection with gas in the left gluteal region (Figure 5). Interventional radiology once again performed percutaneous drainage of the left gluteal (20 ccs of serosanguineous fluid) and right psoas (4 ccs of serosanguinous fluid) collections, with JP drains inserted. Fluid cultures yielded negative results. The patient reported symptom improvement in his left leg evidenced by 4/5 lower extremity strength testing.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Iliopsoas hematoma progression to a psoas abscess, likely due to his immunocompromised status secondary to his uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 40-year-old diabetic male was struck by a vehicle, sustaining a nondisplaced L2 vertebral body fracture with worsening back pain and ambulation difficulties. Initial CT confirmed fracture without acute surgical need. MRI lumbar spine revealed bilateral psoas abscesses and vertebral edema indicating abscess progression likely from prior hematoma. Six days post-presentation, patient developed fever, tachycardia, confusion, elevated WBC, and worsened leg strength, consistent with infection. Interventional radiology drained purulent fluid from left psoas abscess, positive for MSSA. Subsequent CT showed additional fluid collections which were drained, with clinical improvement. The patient was treated with intravenous cefazolin for ten weeks leading to symptomatic resolution.
